Paragraph:
Translation: I do not see how any good can come from killing my own kinsmen in this battle, nor can I, my dear Krsna, desire any subsequent victory, kingdom, or happiness.

Purport (Excerpt): Without knowing that one's self-interest is in Visnu (or Krsna), conditioned souls are attracted by bodily relationships, hoping to be happy in such situations. Under delusion, they forget that Krsna is also the cause of material happiness... Arjuna thought that by killing his kinsmen there would be no happiness in his life, and therefore he was not willing to fight... He has now decided to go into the forest and live a secluded life in frustration.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Deep in cognitive distortion, Arjuna declares that victory and worldly success are meaningless if achieved through the death of his family. He contemplates abandoning his duty entirely to live a life of isolation.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Arjuna verbalizes his complete loss of motivation. He mistakenly equates his ultimate happiness with the survival of his physical family, rather than the execution of his righteous duty. He contemplates the 'flight' response—fleeing to the forest in frustration.
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna's resolve is entirely broken; he actively considers abandoning his societal role and fleeing from his problems.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.depression: Anhedonia (inability to feel pleasure in future prospects), Hopelessness

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Vairagya (False renunciation; attempting to renounce duty out of frustration rather than genuine spiritual detachment)
Ajnana (Ignorance of one's true spiritual self-interest)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Arjuna exhibits 'Markata Vairagya' (monkey renunciation)—a desire to give up the world not out of enlightenment, but out of material frustration and pain. He forgets that true happiness stems from serving the Divine, not from preserving temporary bodily relationships.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This represents a severe depressive symptom: anhedonia coupled with an avoidance coping mechanism. Arjuna's brain, overloaded by the anticipated trauma, shuts down all desire for future reward (kingdom, happiness). To escape the acute distress, he fantasizes about total withdrawal and isolation (fleeing to the forest).
